claims.text: A key alloying element such as Al or Cr preferentially diffuses to the surface of a high-temperature HEA.
The surface-enriched element forms a continuous, adherent, protective oxide layer.
High mixing entropy promotes a uniform elemental distribution in the alloy.
Uniform elemental distribution and favorable diffusion kinetics lead to selective formation of the protective oxide.
The selectively formed oxide reduces further oxygen ingress.
The proposed initial material is an equimolar HEA with a uniformly distributed oxidation-resistant element.
Reducing the concentration of the critical element provides a controlled comparison with the standard-composition alloy.
Heat treatment could be used to enhance or retard surface diffusion of the critical element.
The relevant structural mediator is a dense, surface-localized oxide scale enriched in Al or Cr.
The enriched oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
High entropy causes the critical element to diffuse faster to the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
The critical element oxidizes at the surface to form a low-diffusivity oxide.
A lower concentration of the critical element will produce a less continuous or thinner oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
A less protective scale in the reduced-element alloy will result in greater weight gain and a higher oxidation rate.
The standard equimolar baseline reliably forms a protective oxide layer at high temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies under oxidizing conditions around 1000 degrees Celsius and may not apply at lower temperature or in non-oxidizing environments.
Protective behavior depends on the critical-element concentration and on processing that ensures homogeneous elemental distribution.
Comparable scale continuity, scale composition, and oxidation rates in the standard and reduced-element alloys would falsify the proposed governing role of selective oxidation.
